# Projects vs Custom GPTs for Federal Employees

<!-- vimeo: 1216136134 | track: English (auto-generated) -->

[▶ Watch on Vimeo](https://vimeo.com/1216136134)

<details>
<summary>자막: Projects vs Custom GPTs for Federal Employees</summary>

Federal employees can use both projects and custom GPTs to give ChatGPT specialized context, but they solve different problems. A custom GPT packages repeatable expertise. A project supports work that develops over time. The right choice depends on whether you are reusing a method or continuing a mission workflow. Begin in your authorized ChatGPT workspace. On desktop, open ChatGPT from the top left menu, then choose Chat or Work at the top of the page. On web or mobile, select Work. Your recent conversations and projects appear in the sidebar. Custom GPTs are accessed separately through Explore GPTs, a direct link, or a GPT shared in your workspace. Exact labels and availability can depend on your plan, workspace settings, permissions, and rollout. First, consider a custom GPT. From the sidebar, open Explore GPTs. Choose an approved workspace GPT, or if your role and workspace settings permit, open My GPTs and select Create. This fictional program briefing assistant contains stable instructions, an approved briefing format, standard terminology, and a few conversation starters. Any authorized employee can use the same configured method, attach the current program results, and ask for three executive takeaways. This is useful when the expertise should remain consistent across many assignments. Now return one month later. The briefing method still works, but the assignment has changed. There is new performance data, a revised policy memo, leadership feedback, a decision from the previous review, and a teammate's analysis. A new conversation with the custom GPT does not automatically draw on the previous conversation. The employee must provide the current assignment context again. The expertise persisted. The evolving work history did not. For that continuing body of work, open Work and select New Project in the sidebar. Name the fictional project Fiscal Year 26 Service Delivery Review. Then choose an icon and color. Open the project and start a work thread using the project's context. In project settings, add instructions that apply only inside this project. For example, use only authorized sources, separate verified facts from inference, cite quantitative claims, identify missing information, and never invent figures, citations, owners, or decisions. Next, add the materials that define the work, the June baseline briefing, July performance spreadsheet, leadership meeting notes, and updated implementation policy. Move in any eligible prior chat that belongs with the assignment. Then organize separate threads for establishing the baseline, analyzing performance, incorporating leadership feedback, and preparing the decision briefing. Projects keep related chats, files, and instructions together. When sharing is enabled by your organization, teammates can contribute context and continue the work together. Shared project permissions determine who can chat, edit sources, or invite others. Now ask Work to update the leadership brief using the July report and the deputy director's feedback. Compare the results with the June baseline, identify what changed and what remains uncertain, and cite the project source for every quantitative claim. The project can carry the accumulated context into this new thread. The employee reviews the evidence, corrects any gaps, and completes the required human approval. Use a custom GPT when the method repeats. Use a project when the work evolves. In either case, use only information authorized for your environment. Follow agency data handling requirements and verify consequential claims before you brief, send, or act.
